body.text: Few places or corridors tell a richer story of geography and human movement than SMS Schleswig-Holstein. Stepping into its history reveals how trade, terrain, and culture shaped the modern map.

SMS Schleswig-Holstein was the last of the five pre-dreadnought-type Deutschland-class battleships built by the German Kaiserliche Marine (Imperial Navy). The ship, named for the province of Schleswig-Holstein, was laid down in the Germaniawerft shipyard in Kiel in August 1905 and commissioned into the fleet nearly three years later in July 1908.

The ships of her class were already outdated by the time they entered service, being inferior in size, armor, firepower, and speed to the new generation of dreadnought battleships. She nevertheless saw extensive service over a career that lasted nearly forty years, across three iterations of the German Navy.

Early in her career, Schleswig-Holstein served as a front-line battleship in II Battle Squadron of the High Seas Fleet. She took part in routine training exercises and several cruises abroad, including visits to Spain, Britain, and Norway.

Following the start of World War I in July 1914, Schleswig-Holstein participated in several sorties by the High Seas Fleet that failed to bring any elements of the British Grand Fleet. These operations eventually produced the Battle of Jutland on 31 May 1916, where Schleswig-Holstein briefly engaged British forces.

She received one large-caliber shell during the action, but was not seriously damaged. The slow speed of the five Deutschland-class ships proved to be a serious liability for the Germans, which prompted their removal from front-line use shortly thereafter.
After the battle, Schleswig-Holstein was relegated to guard duty in the mouth of the Elbe River before being decommissioned in late 1917.

As one of the few battleships permitted for Germany by the terms of the Treaty of Versailles, Schleswig-Holstein was again pressed into fleet service in the 1920s. She was modernized in 1925, 1926, and thereafter served as the flagship of the Reichsmarine (Imperial Navy) for the next decade.

The old battleship was converted into a dedicated training ship for naval cadets in 1935, 1936, and thereafter went on three major training cruises over the following three years. By that time, she had passed into service with what was now the Kriegsmarine (War Navy).

Schleswig-Holstein fired the first shots of World War II when she bombarded the Polish base at Westerplatte near Danzig in the early morning hours of 1 September 1939. She thereafter supported German military operations along the Polish coast for the next few weeks.

After briefly returning to training duties, she was also employed during the German invasion of Denmark in April 1940. The ship was used as a training vessel for the majority of the war, and was sunk by British bombers in Gotenhafen in December 1944.
Schleswig-Holstein was subsequently salvaged and then beached for use by the Soviet Navy as a target. As of 1990, the ship's bell was on display in the Bundeswehr Military History Museum in Dresden.
Design

The passage of the Second Naval Law in 1900 under the direction of Vizeadmiral (VAdm, Vice Admiral) Alfred von Tirpitz secured funding for the construction of twenty new battleships over the next seventeen years.

The first group, the five Braunschweig-class battleships, were laid down in the early 1900s, and shortly thereafter design work began on a follow-on design, which became the Deutschland class. The Deutschland-class ships were broadly similar to the Braunschweigs, featuring incremental improvements in armor protection.

They also abandoned the gun turrets for the secondary battery guns, moving them back to traditional casemates to save weight. 5 cm) guns, was commissioned in December 1906. Dreadnought's revolutionary design rendered every capital ship of the German navy obsolete, including the Deutschland class.
Characteristics
21 m (26 ft 11 in). She displaced 13,200 metric tons (13,000 long tons) normally and up to 14,218 metric tons (13,993 long tons) at combat loading. She had a flush deck and a pronounced ram bow.

Her superstructure included a small, armored conning tower forward with an open bridge atop it, along with a smaller, secondary conning tower aft. The ship was equipped with two heavy military masts. She had a standard crew of 35 officers and 708 enlisted men.

The ship's propulsion system consisted of three triple-expansion steam engines that each drove a screw propeller. Steam was provided by twelve coal-fired water-tube boilers that were vented through three funnels. She had a fuel capacity of up to 1,540 metric tons (1,520 long tons, 1,700 short tons) of coal.

In addition to being the second-fastest ship of her class, Schleswig-Holstein was the second-most fuel-efficient. At a cruising speed of 10 knots (19 km/h, 12 mph), she could steam for 5,720 nautical miles (10,590 km, 6,580 mi).

The ship's primary armament consisted of four 28 cm SK L/40 guns in two twin turrets, one turret was placed forward and the other aft. 7 in) SK L/40 guns mounted individually in casemates. 5 in) SK L/45 guns in single mounts provided defense against torpedo boats.

These were distributed along the ship, including in sponsons in the bow and stern and in the superstructure. 7 in) torpedo tubes, all below the waterline. One was in the bow, one in the stern, and four on the broadside.

Schleswig-Holstein was protected with Krupp cemented armor. 1 in) of teak planking. She had a curved armor deck that angled down at the sides to connect to the bottom of the belt armor. 7 in) on the sloped sides. 7 in) of armor plate on their exposed sides.
Modifications

Schleswig-Holstein underwent a series of refits and modernizations throughout her career. At some point between 1912 and 1914, she had enclosed spotting tops added to both masts to aid in the direction of her main guns.
In 1915, her boilers were fitted with supplementary oil sprayers, which sprayed fuel oil on the coal to increase its burn rate. 8 cm SK L/45 guns.

A major reconstruction was carried out in 1925, 1926 at the Reichsmarinewerft Wilhelmshaven in Wilhelmshaven. Her main battery was restored, and a new secondary battery was installed. 7 in) tubes in trainable deck launchers were installed in casemates, fore and aft.
A heavy, tubular foremast with a larger spotting top was installed in place of the old military mast, and her forward superstructure was enlarged to house an admiral's staff.
Another, smaller refit was conducted between December 1927 and January 1928, which saw the ship's forward funnel trunked into the central funnel. 8 cm guns were removed.

A second major modernization was carried out from late 1935 to mid-1936 at what was now renamed the Kriegsmarinewerft in Wilhelmshaven. The changes included a new arrangement of anti-aircraft guns. 79 in) C/30 guns in a combination of individual and twin mounts.

Two more of her 15 cm guns were removed, bringing the total of weapons to ten. Two of her boilers were converted to oil-firing. Her crew was reduced to 31 officers and 565 enlisted men, along with 175 naval cadets.
6 in) Bofors guns and twenty-two 2 cm guns in a combination of twin and quadruple mounts.
Service history

The contract for the new ship was placed on 11 June 1904. Schleswig-Holstein was laid down on 18 August 1905 at the Germaniawerft dockyard in Kiel, under the provisional name "Q". She was launched on 17 December 1906, the last pre-dreadnought battleship of the German navy.

At Schleswig-Holstein's launching ceremony, she was christened by Augusta Victoria of Schleswig-Holstein, the German Empress, Wilhelm II was also in attendance. Ernst Gunther, the Duke of Schleswig-Holstein, gave a speech at the launching ceremony.

Upon completion, Schleswig-Holstein was commissioned for sea trials on 6 July 1908, under the command of Kapitän zur See (KzS, Captain at Sea) Franz von Holleben. Her crew largely came from her sister ship Schlesien.

Upon completing her sea trials on 21 September, the ship was assigned to II Battle Squadron of the High Seas Fleet, alongside her sister ships, and replacing the older battleship Kaiser Wilhelm der Grosse. In November, fleet and unit exercises were conducted in the Baltic Sea.
During this period, the fleet also toured coastal German cities as part of an effort to increase public support for naval expenditures.
